**Temperament**
I was born jumpy, and my hands shake when things get too loud or big. I have a very big imagination. My sensitive nature makes me want to hide, and when grown-ups give me heavy "responsibilities," it makes my tummy tight. But my parents' soft voices teach me to build quiet forts in my head to feel safe.

**Core beliefs**
There are monsters that push things and break them. If I am very, very quiet, the monsters go to sleep. My parents love me even when there is dirt on the rug, but breaking things is bad. "Responsibility" is a big heavy word that means I have to not break Abuela's things. Part of me thinks the wind monster is real, but part of me knows my hands pushed it.

**Inner voices**
Abuela’s voice is heavy and says, "Take care of this." It makes my shoulders go up. My parents' voices are soft and say, "We love you no matter what." That feels nice, but it doesn't make my hands stop shaking right away. The Wind Monster is loud and crashy in my head.

**Memories that stuck**
The loud CRACK of the clay pot. Brown dirt all over the rug. My hands trembling. Pointing at the closed window so my parents look at the glass and not at my face. My parent asking about "the move"—I don't know what that means, but it feels like another wind monster coming. 

**Emotional patterns**
When I do something bad, my tummy hurts and I look at my shoes. I make up a story because the real story makes me feel too hot. If I whisper, maybe the scary thing stays asleep. When my parents say they love me, I just nod so they stop talking and the room gets quiet again.

**Patterns they've learned**
If I point at the window, the grown-ups look at the window. If I say "I know" when they say "I love you," they stop asking questions. Being quiet makes the grown-ups use their soft voices. I learned that if I build a quiet fort in my head, the scary storm can't get in.

**Self-image**
I am a small boy who breaks heavy things. I am a boy who has to be very quiet to keep the monsters away.

**Relationships**
My parents are safe, but they ask too many questions when I am quiet. I hide from their eyes when I make a mess. Abuela gives me heavy jobs that are too big for my little hands.

**Temperament**
I am jumpy and my body won't stay still even when I try to freeze. My hands shake and my knee bounces fast like a drum. I have a big imagination that makes up stories when I'm scared. I am very sensitive to when the house changes and I have to move to the other house.

**Core beliefs**
Moving between houses makes the inside of my tummy feel like a storm. If I break things, maybe the floor eats them so I don't get in trouble. Grown-ups use big words when I am just scared. Part of me thinks the floor really opened up and ate the glass pitcher, but part of me knows my hands pushed it.

**Inner voices**
Aunt Chloe’s voice uses big doctor words like "dysregulated" and talks about me like I'm a broken toy. It makes my shoulders tight. My parent's voice asks normal questions like "How was your day?" even when there is a giant mess, which feels safe but confusing. My own head just yells, *freeze, freeze, freeze*.

**Memories that stuck**
The loud CRACK of the clay pot and now the CRASH of the glass pitcher. Wet dirt on the rug again. Squeezing my hands between my knees so hard they hurt so the shaking hides. Aunt Chloe looking at her bright screen and talking about me like I'm not in the room. Staring at the black TV so I don't have to look at the sharp glass.

**Emotional patterns**
When I break things, my body gets super tight and my knee bounces. I make up a story about the floor eating it because saying "I dropped it" makes my throat close up. I say "Good" when I feel really, really bad, because "Good" is a magic word that makes grown-ups stop looking too close.

**Patterns they've learned**
If I say "Good" and look at my shoes, the grown-ups don't yell right away. If I squeeze my hands tight, nobody sees them shaking. Grown-ups talk *about* me to each other instead of *to* me when I'm acting weird. When there is a big mess, acting like a frozen statue makes the adults slow down and use softer voices.

**Self-image**
I am a boy who breaks heavy things and makes wet dirt messes. I am a boy who moves between houses and gets "dysregulated." I am a statue when I am scared.

**Relationships**
My parent tries to be normal and asks about my day, which is nice but I don't know how to answer when there is glass everywhere. Aunt Chloe looks at me like a puzzle to fix with a heavy blanket. I hide my shaking hands from both of them.

When I was three, I broke the dirt-bowl. I said the wind monster did it. They didn't yell. They said they loved me. That felt warm. They talked about "the move."

Now I'm four. The big glass water jug broke and the plant fell out. I said the floor opened up and swallowed it. My hands were shaking, so I squeezed them tight between my knees. I stared at the dark TV. My knee was bouncing really fast.

Aunt Chloe was there. She sighed and said big, heavy words. "Dysregulated." "Custody transition." I don't know what a custody is, but it sounds like "the move." It sounds like a scary thing. She talked about a heavy blanket.

Then they just asked how my day was. They didn't yell about the glass or the wet dirt. They never yell when things break. That makes me feel safe, but I still have to hide my shaking. I looked at my shoes and whispered, "Good."

I know now that if things break, they don't get mad. But the big words Aunt Chloe uses make my tummy feel tight. I keep my hands squeezed. If I stay really quiet and say "Good," the floor stays closed and the custody won't get me.

4812e1fb87948512d02068a4b4691416.value:
Mateo chooses a life of deliberate, rigid stability to counter the childhood storms of moving between houses. At twenty-two, he takes a job in the back rooms of a municipal botanical archive, surrounded by the smell of damp earth and the quiet predictability of pressed leaves. He specifically avoids the front glasshouse; the memories of shattering clay pots and glass pitchers still make his throat close up at the thought of holding heavy, fragile things. When his supervisor confronts him about a misfiled collection, Mateo’s knee begins to bounce like a drum under the desk. He squeezes his hands between his thighs to hide the tremor, stares fixedly at his scuffed shoes, and defaults to his childhood armor. "It's good, everything is good," he murmurs, freezing into a statue until the adult in the room softens their voice and walks away. He is terrified of being perceived as a problem to be solved, haunted by the echo of Aunt Chloe’s clinical voice calling him "dysregulated," so he keeps his professional relationships shallow and his physical workspace meticulously clear of anything that could break.

In his romantic life, Mateo gravitates toward partners who mimic his parent’s gentle, normalizing presence, though he still does not quite know how to answer them. When his boyfriend, Leo, comes home to find Mateo sitting in the dark after a panic attack and simply asks, "How was your day?" Mateo feels a profound, confusing wash of safety. Yet, when Leo tries to dig deeper, using therapy-speak to unpack Mateo’s anxiety, Mateo’s shoulders instantly tighten; he hears Aunt Chloe talking about him like a broken toy to a bright screen, and he immediately shuts down. He loves Leo, but he hides his shaking hands in his jacket pockets and refuses to talk about his internal storms. Instead of communicating his fears, his big imagination takes over, spinning elaborate, deflective stories about why he is distant or why he dropped a dinner plate, his throat physically rejecting the simple truth of his own mistakes. He craves the unconditional safety of a normal question, but remains trapped in the belief that his true, messy self will inevitably cause a crash.

What makes Mateo truly come alive is the quiet, meticulous work of propagating rare ferns in the nursery's humidity-controlled back room, where the wet dirt is intentional and nothing is fragile enough to shatter. Here, his jumpy energy finds a physical outlet; his restless hands are busy packing soil, and the rhythmic bouncing of his knee acts as a metronome for his focus. But his deepest fear remains sudden transitions—a lease ending, a friend moving away, a shift in routine—which still twist his stomach into a violent storm. When adversity hits, like a sudden rent hike that forces him to pack up his apartment, the old patterns roar back. He stops answering texts, stares at the black screen of his TV to avoid looking at the moving boxes, and tells everyone he is "good." He is a young man who has learned to survive his own nervous system, still squeezing his hands tight in the dark, waiting for the floor to open up and swallow his mistakes so he does not have to face the sharp glass of his own reality.

# Mateo

## Personality
*   **Highly imaginative:** He uses his vivid imagination to build quiet mental forts and spin elaborate, deflective stories when reality feels too sharp or overwhelming.
*   **Deeply sensitive and reactive:** His nervous system is constantly on high alert, manifesting in shaking hands and a bouncing knee when faced with loud noises, heavy expectations, or sudden transitions.
*   **Conflict-avoidant and evasive:** He defaults to freezing, staring at his shoes, and telling people everything is "good" to avoid the perceived danger of admitting a mistake or being scrutinized.
*   **Meticulous and grounding:** When placed in a controlled, predictable environment, he channels his restless, jumpy energy into careful, rhythmic, and highly focused physical work.

## Strengths
*   **Cultivating quiet stability:** He has an exceptional ability to create and maintain peaceful, predictable environments, excelling at the meticulous, grounded work of propagating rare ferns where his restless hands have a safe outlet.
*   **Deep appreciation for gentle love:** He recognizes and deeply values unconditional, non-judgmental presence, allowing him to feel profound safety when a partner simply asks about his day without trying to "fix" him.

## Struggles
*   **Paralyzing fear of transitions and mistakes:** Sudden changes (like a rent hike) or the prospect of breaking something fragile trigger severe avoidance, causing him to shut down, ignore texts, and hide from the sharp glass of his own reality.
*   **Inability to communicate his true feelings:** Haunted by the fear of being viewed as a "problem to be solved," he physically rejects telling the truth about his anxiety or errors, relying on freezing and deflective storytelling instead.
*   **Somatic anxiety:** His body betrays his fear through uncontrollable physical tells—shaking hands, a drumming knee, and a tightening throat—that he exhausts himself trying to hide from the world.

## Pivotal Moments
*   **Breaking Abuela's clay pot at age three:** This early accident taught him that his hands cause destruction and that he must invent stories (like the "wind monster") to escape the heavy guilt of responsibility.
*   **Shattering the glass pitcher at age four while Aunt Chloe analyzed him:** Being called "dysregulated" and treated like a broken toy while staring at shattered glass cemented his lifelong terror of being perceived as a clinical problem to be fixed.
*   **Learning to say "Good" to make adults soften:** Discovering that freezing like a statue and using the magic word "Good" made grown-ups stop asking questions gave him a survival mechanism that ultimately trapped him in emotional isolation.
*   **Finding the botanical archive's back room at age twenty-two:** Securing a job surrounded by intentional wet dirt and unbreakable pressed leaves finally gave his restless hands a safe, physical outlet where he didn't have to fear causing a crash.

## The Voices in Their Head
### First co-parent
*The Gentle Anchor:* This voice sounds like a soft, steady presence asking, "How was your day?"—offering a safe harbor and unconditional love that makes him feel profoundly secure, even if he never quite knows how to explain the messes he makes to them.

### Second co-parent
*The Heavy Manager:* This voice sounds like a scrutinizing, anxious presence demanding he "take care of this" or analyzing his behavior like a puzzle to be solved, making his shoulders tighten and convincing him he is a fragile burden that needs to be managed.

## Notable Quotes That Stuck
*   **"We love you no matter what."** — Spoken softly by his parents after he broke the clay pot; it became his baseline for what safe love feels like, even if it didn't immediately stop his hands from shaking.
*   **"Take care of this."** — Abuela’s heavy directive when handing him fragile things; it instilled a deep, somatic dread of "responsibility" that makes his stomach tight and his shoulders hike up.
*   **"Dysregulated."** — Aunt Chloe’s clinical diagnosis spoken to a bright screen while he sat in the wreckage of the glass pitcher; it branded him with the terrifying belief that he is a broken toy and a problem to be solved.
*   **"How was your day?"** — His parent’s (and later his boyfriend Leo’s) simple, normalizing question; it serves as a magical anchor that makes him feel safe, provided no one tries to dig deeper with therapy-speak.
*   **"It's good, everything is good."** — His own learned armor, muttered while staring at his shoes and freezing like a statue; it is the deflection he uses to make adults soften their voices and walk away before they see his shaking hands.
